topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Sound waves (physics only) (HT only)
subject: physics

items.q: A hammer strikes one end of a long steel rail. A student with an ear pressed against the far end hears the blow. What is happening inside the steel as the sound travels along it?
items.correct: Particles of the steel vibrate about their positions and pass the disturbance on
items.misconception: Sound slips along the tiny gaps of air trapped between the steel particles
items.why: Sound is first met as a wave in air, so students keep air as the only thing that can really carry it and look for a route for the air to follow through the solid. No air path is needed. The specification states that sound waves travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid — the solid is the medium, not an obstacle with holes in it.
items.random_wrong: Sound leaves the rail at once and reaches the ear through the air

items.q: Music from a loudspeaker in one room can be heard through a solid brick wall in the room next door. Which statement best describes the part the wall plays?
items.correct: The brick itself vibrates and carries the sound wave to the far side
items.misconception: It blocks the sound entirely, so what is heard has leaked round the edges
items.why: Students learn correctly that sound cannot travel through a vacuum and then compress 'sound needs a medium' into 'sound needs air', which makes every solid a barrier rather than a carrier. A medium is anything made of particles. Solids carry sound well because their particles are close together and strongly linked, which is why a hammer blow is heard clearly along a long steel rail.
items.random_wrong: Sound seeps through the pores of trapped air inside the brick

items.q: A sound wave travelling through the air arrives at a person's ear. Which statement describes how this leads to the sensation of sound?
items.correct: The wave makes the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
items.misconception: The ear drum turns the wave straight into electricity and never moves
items.why: Biology lessons emphasise nerve impulses and the brain, so the mechanical step is skipped and the frequency limit is blamed on the brain rather than on the conversion. The mechanical step comes first and is where the limit lies: the wave must set solid parts of the ear vibrating, and that conversion only works over a limited frequency range.
items.random_wrong: The wave passes on unchanged along the ear canal and into the brain

items.q: A bat call at 45 kHz is played to a class through an ultrasonic transducer at very high intensity. Nobody in the room hears anything. What is the best explanation?
items.correct: The ear cannot convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations
items.misconception: The sound is far too quiet by the time that it has reached anybody's ear
items.why: Everyday experience of turning up a volume control makes amplitude the obvious explanation for audibility, and frequency is rarely offered as a separate limit. The limit is a frequency limit, not an amplitude limit. Above about 20 kHz the parts of the ear cannot be driven into useful vibration, so raising the intensity does not create the sensation of sound.
items.random_wrong: A 45 kHz pressure wave in air is not a sound wave, so there is nothing to hear

items.q: A singer's voice is picked up by a microphone and played back through a loudspeaker. Which statement correctly describes what happens at the microphone diaphragm and at the loudspeaker cone?
items.correct: Sound waves set the diaphragm vibrating, and the vibrating cone makes sound waves
items.misconception: Both the diaphragm and the cone turn a sound wave into vibrations of a solid
items.why: The ear drum is met first and is stored as a one-way example, so the process is remembered as 'sound in, vibration out' rather than as a reversible conversion. The specification asks for processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids — between, in either direction, as a loudspeaker shows.
items.random_wrong: The diaphragm vibrates the air, while the cone stops the air vibrating

items.q: A drum is struck in a hall and a listener standing a few metres away in the air hears the beat. Which sequence of events describes what happens?
items.correct: The skin vibrates, a sound wave crosses the air, and the ear drum vibrates
items.misconception: The drum skin passes its vibrations along the floor and into the listener
items.why: Students learn correctly that sound cannot travel through a vacuum and then compress 'sound needs a medium' into 'sound needs air', which makes every solid a barrier rather than a carrier. A medium is anything made of particles. Solids carry sound well because their particles are close together and strongly linked, which is why a hammer blow is heard clearly along a long steel rail.
items.random_wrong: Air vibrates first, then the drum skin vibrates, and then the beat is heard

items.q: Explain why the process by which the ear detects sound works only over a limited frequency range, and what this means for what a person can hear.
items.correct: Sound waves outside a limited band cannot be converted into vibrations of the ear's solid parts
items.misconception: Outside that band no sound wave exists at all, so there is simply nothing arriving at the ear to detect
items.why: The audible range is taught as 'the range of sound', so students treat a limit on human perception as a limit on the physics itself. 20 Hz to 20 kHz is the range of normal human hearing, not the range of sound. Ultrasound and infrasound are sound waves that the human ear cannot convert.
items.random_wrong: The brain selects the frequencies it accepts, so the ear itself passes on every sound wave arriving

items.q: What is the range of normal human hearing?
items.why: Prefixes are handled by feel rather than by value, and both limits of hearing begin with the digits '20', which invites students to guess at the scaling between them. kilo means x1000 every time. 20 Hz is the lower limit and 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz is the upper limit, so the two limits are a factor of a thousand apart.

items.q: Does human hearing have a lower frequency limit?
items.correct: Yes. Normal human hearing runs from 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so there is a lower limit as well as an upper one.
items.misconception: Only very high frequencies lie outside human hearing; low frequencies can always be heard, so there is no lower limit.
items.why: Ultrasound and dog whistles dominate the teaching of the audible range, and very low frequencies are felt as well as heard, which blurs the lower boundary. The conversion in the ear fails at both ends of the range. Below 20 Hz a wave may be felt as a vibration but it does not produce the sensation of sound.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.1.4 Waves in air, fluids and solids: Sound waves (physics only) (HT only)
